analysis.answer: Current law allows parents of eligible public-school children to receive 90 percent of state per-pupil funding in an education savings account to pay for private educational alternatives. This measure completely repeals that program on July 1, 2028, and sends any unspent funds back to the public school system.

Families who currently use or plan to use education savings accounts for private tuition bear the cost by losing this financial support. Public schools and the state school fund benefit by retaining the per-pupil funding that would have otherwise gone to private educational accounts, as well as absorbing any leftover balances.

Families relying on the accounts may move their children back to public schools if they cannot afford private tuition out of pocket. In the years leading up to the 2028 deadline, parents might accelerate their spending of account balances on eligible services to avoid forfeiting the funds. Private schools and tutors that cater to ESA recipients may experience reduced enrollment and revenue.

The measure addresses concerns that education savings accounts divert vital resources and students away from the public school system. By repealing the program, it conversely removes a mechanism that provided lower- and middle-income families with financial access to private education, potentially recreating barriers to school choice.
Public school districts gain resources and potentially student enrollment that would have otherwise left for private options.

Researchers disagree on the overall effects of education savings accounts and voucher programs. Some studies indicate that such programs improve academic outcomes for participants and exert competitive pressure that lifts public school performance. Other research finds negative or neutral academic effects for participants and argues that these programs harm public schools by draining their financial resources and altering their student demographics.
The state will incur administrative costs to audit and close all active education savings accounts, and to successfully transfer remaining balances to the state school fund by the 2028 deadline.
This is a statutory repeal and could be undone by future legislation or a ballot initiative reinstating the program.
